title: Asante: The Kingdom of the Golden Stool

pages.text: On an Akwasidae Sunday at Manhyia Palace in Kumasi, the great drums sound and a sea of umbrellas moves across the courtyard. Chiefs in rich kente take their seats. Then a stool covered in gold is carried out and set on its own chair, beside the king. Nobody sits on it, not even the Asantehene. This is the Golden Stool, and to the Asante it holds the soul of the whole nation. To understand why a stool matters more than a throne, go back more than three hundred years, to a time when there was no Asante kingdom at all.

pages.text: In the late 1600s, the forest around Kumasi was home to several small Akan states, such as Kwaman, Mampong, Bekwai, Juaben, and Nsuta. Each had its own chief. All of them paid tribute to a powerful southern neighbour, Denkyira, which was rich in gold. The chief of Kwaman was a young man named Osei Tutu. He had spent years at the courts of Denkyira and Akwamu and had seen how strong states were run. His closest adviser was a priest, Okomfo Anokye. Together they planned to turn a group of small states into one nation.

pages.alt: Several small forest towns linked by footpaths, with one larger town in the centre.

pages.text: Tradition tells what happened next. On a Friday, Okomfo Anokye called the chiefs together at Kumasi. Before them all, a golden stool came down from the sky and settled gently on the knees of Osei Tutu. Anokye declared that it held the spirit of all their people: the living, the dead, and those not yet born. Whatever a historian makes of the story, its meaning was plain to the chiefs. They no longer belonged only to their own towns. They were one people with one king, the Asantehene. Around 1701, their united army defeated Denkyira at Feyiase. Asante was free.

They no longer belonged only to their own towns.
They were one people with one king, the Asantehene.
Around 1701, their united army defeated Denkyira at Feyiase.
Asante was free.
pages.alt: A gathering of chiefs seated in a circle beneath tall trees, looking up towards a bright light.

pages.text: Over the next century, Asante grew into one of the strongest states in West Africa. Under Opoku Ware and later kings, its power reached north to Gonja and Dagbon and south towards the coast. Great roads ran out from Kumasi in every direction, and officials travelled them to collect taxes and carry messages. Gold and kola nuts went north to the savanna markets. Laws were made in a council of chiefs, and the queen mother had a strong voice in choosing each king. Weavers at Bonwire made kente, and craftsmen at Ntonso stamped adinkra cloth.

pages.text: Asante’s growth brought it into conflict with Britain, which was taking control of the coast. They fought several wars in the 1800s. In 1824, Asante won a famous victory. In 1874, a British army burned Kumasi. In 1896, the British seized the Asantehene, Prempeh I, and sent him far away to the Seychelles islands. Then, in 1900, the British governor demanded the Golden Stool to sit on. The chiefs hesitated. Yaa Asantewaa, queen mother of Ejisu, did not. She led the army in a last war. Asante was defeated, but the stool had been hidden, and it was never captured.

pages.text: Prempeh I came home in 1924, and in 1935 the Asante union was restored. Today Ghana is a republic with an elected president, yet the Asantehene still sits at Manhyia, settles disputes, and supports schools and health care. The Golden Stool is still brought out on great days. What does the story teach? A nation is more than land and soldiers. It needs something that all its members agree to honour: a shared idea. For Asante, that idea took the shape of a stool. For Ghana today, it is a flag, an anthem, and a constitution.

activities.question: Before Asante was united, what did the small states around Kumasi have in common?
options: They all paid tribute to Denkyira
They were all ruled from the coast

activities.question: What did the Golden Stool mean to the chiefs?
options: It was a gift for the king of Denkyira
It showed that they were now one people with one king
It was a seat for the Asantehene to sit on

activities.question: Why did war break out in 1900?
options: The British governor demanded the Golden Stool

activities.question: Apply it: The article says a nation needs a shared idea that all its members honour. Which of these plays that part for Ghana today?
options: The national flag, anthem, and constitution
